lessons.name: Aero-200
lessons.summary: Aero-200 is Dufour Aerospace’s hybrid-electric cargo drone, designed to take off vertically and cruise on wings.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence
Aero-200 is Dufour Aerospace’s hybrid-electric cargo drone, designed to take off vertically and cruise on wings.

![Dufour’s published Aero-200 product rendering showing the wing tilted into different flight positions](/img/lessons/robots_drone-aero-200.webp)
*Dufour’s published Aero-200 product rendering showing the wing tilted into different flight positions. Source: [Dufour Aerospace](https://www.dufour.aero/aero-200), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us
- **A flying delivery system:** Dufour proposes transporting blood, medicines and urgent spare parts without needing a runway at each endpoint.
- **A control problem:** software must handle hovering, forward flight and the transition between them, rather than treating every part of a journey identically.

## What it is made of / how it works
- **Tilt-wing:** the whole wing changes orientation; propellers provide vertical lift at take-off and forward propulsion during cruise.
- **Hybrid-electric power:** the published powertrain combines electric propulsion with a gasoline-fuelled two-stroke engine for longer missions.
- **Software analogy:** think of a state machine with take-off, transition, cruise and landing states; each state needs different control behaviour.
- **Worked example:** Dufour’s typical mission is 20 kg over 200 km; that differs from its 38 kg useful-load limit, which is not a range guarantee.
- **Manufacturer figures:** the table describes the advertised design; the current product page schedules serial-production aircraft for 2027.

| Specification | Published value |
| --- | --- |
| Wingspan | 6.12 m |
| Maximum take-off mass | 208 kg |
| Useful load | 38 kg |
| Typical mission | 20 kg / 200 km |
| Efficient cruise speed | 125 km/h |
| Fuel | Gasoline |

> **Key idea:** Flight mode and payload belong in the mission specification, because a single maximum number cannot describe the whole journey.

## Key terms
- **VTOL**: vertical take-off and landing, without a take-off run along a runway.
- **Useful load**: the load budget available beyond the aircraft’s own basic mass.
- **Flight computer**: the onboard computer running the aircraft’s control software.
- **Telemetry**: measurements sent from the aircraft to its operator.

## Getting started
1. **Access:** hardware price and student access are unknown; the product page and brochure are free to read.
2. **Sketch** a civilian medical delivery with departure, cruise and arrival states, using the published typical mission as a reference.
3. **Build** a tiny software state machine that rejects a cruise command until its transition state completes; use simulated inputs only.
4. **Compare** your state diagram with the manufacturer’s transition demonstration, which shows tilt-wing behaviour rather than a production performance test.

## Used in
- **Builder:** Dufour Aerospace develops the avionics, flight-control software and mission-control systems described in its brochure.
- **Compare:** WingtraRAY also combines vertical departure with wing-borne travel, but collects surveying data instead of delivering cargo.

lessons.name: ANAFI UKR
lessons.summary: ANAFI UKR is Parrot’s compact observation drone, combining stabilised visible-light and thermal cameras with onboard navigation and multiple communication links.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence
ANAFI UKR is Parrot’s compact observation drone, combining stabilised visible-light and thermal cameras with onboard navigation and multiple communication links.

![ANAFI UKR hovering beside its controller and equipment case in Parrot’s product image](/img/lessons/robots_drone-anafi-ukr.webp)
*ANAFI UKR hovering beside its controller and equipment case in Parrot’s product image. Source: [Parrot](https://www.parrot.com/en/anafi-ukr), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us
- **More than video:** the aircraft has to estimate its motion, stabilise its cameras and maintain communication while producing usable observations.
- **A useful systems case:** its separate sensing, navigation and radio components make a concrete example of software depending on physical measurements.

## What it is made of / how it works
- **Navigation sensors:** satellite receivers, inertial sensors, a pressure sensor and stereo cameras help the aircraft estimate movement and surroundings.
- **Camera gimbal:** a motorised mount stabilises the visible and thermal cameras while the aircraft moves.
- **Software analogy:** model navigation and video as separate services; a clear image does not prove the location estimate is trustworthy.
- **Worked example:** the Standard battery claim is 38 minutes at 6 m/s airspeed; the XLR claim is 70 minutes at 6.5 m/s.
- **Configuration matters:** these are Parrot’s current technical-page figures, with different battery masses and test conditions.

| Specification | Published value |
| --- | --- |
| Standard-battery aircraft mass | Less than 1,033 g |
| XLR-battery aircraft mass | Less than 1,365 g |
| Maximum take-off mass | 1,450 g |
| Maximum flight time, Standard | 38 min at 6 m/s airspeed |
| Maximum flight time, XLR | 70 min at 6.5 m/s airspeed |
| Visible video | 4K or Full HD |
| Gimbal tilt | −90° to +90° |

> **Key idea:** Battery, sensing and communication choices change what a mission can achieve, even when the aircraft name stays the same.

## Key terms
- **Thermal camera**: an imager that detects infrared radiation rather than visible colours.
- **IMU**: an inertial measurement unit sensing acceleration and rotation.
- **Stereo cameras**: paired cameras whose different views support depth estimation.
- **Airspeed**: speed relative to the surrounding air, which differs from speed over the ground.

## Getting started
1. **Access:** public tutorials and the user guide are free; current delivered hardware price is unknown.
2. **Watch** the aircraft brief and identify the camera assembly, battery and controller before reading the technical table.
3. **Create** two configuration records for Standard and XLR batteries; keep each mass and endurance claim attached to its own battery.
4. **Read** the guide’s navigation and pre-flight sections, then explain which observations your mock software would need before declaring itself ready.

## Used in
- **Builder:** Parrot supplies ANAFI UKR and documents it through FreeFlight 8 tutorials and the user guide.
- **Compare:** Fotokite Sigma provides an elevated visible/thermal view through a tethered system with a much more constrained operating area.

lessons.name: Bitcraze Crazyflie 2.1
lessons.summary: Bitcraze Crazyflie 2.1 is a palm-sized open-source quadcopter whose published hardware and firmware expose the basics of multirotor flight control.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence
Bitcraze Crazyflie 2.1 is a palm-sized open-source quadcopter whose published hardware and firmware expose the basics of multirotor flight control.

![The original Crazyflie 2.1 with four small propellers, exposed electronics and a battery on top](/img/lessons/robots_drone-crazyflie-21.webp)
*The original Crazyflie 2.1 with four small propellers, exposed electronics and a battery on top. Source: [Bitcraze](https://www.bitcraze.io/products/old-products/crazyflie-2-1/), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us
- **A readable robot:** its firmware repository lets a software student inspect the path from a command to a motor output.
- **Model identity matters:** Bitcraze’s August 2024 announcement discontinued 2.1 in favour of 2.1+; use the archived specifications for this older node.

## What it is made of / how it works
- **Four motors:** changing their relative thrust tilts the aircraft; total thrust helps it rise or descend.
- **Onboard sensors:** an accelerometer and gyroscope measure movement; a pressure sensor supports altitude estimation.
- **Control loop:** software repeatedly compares a requested attitude with an estimated attitude and updates motor commands.
- **Software analogy:** the high-level client sends requests, while a fast onboard worker handles stabilisation instead of waiting for each computer message.
- **Worked example:** 7 minutes × 60 = 420 seconds of advertised flight time; this conversion is a planning illustration, not usable experimental airtime.
- **Archived manufacturer figures:** accessories and positioning decks change the flying configuration.

| Specification | Published value |
| --- | --- |
| Mass on archived product page | 29 g |
| Advertised flight time | 7 min |
| Maximum recommended payload | 15 g |
| Main processor | STM32F405, 168 MHz |
| Inertial sensing | 3-axis accelerometer and 3-axis gyroscope |
| Pressure sensor | BMP388 |

> **Key idea:** Onboard stabilisation and commands from your program run at different levels of the robot’s control system.

> **Watch out:** Small propellers can still cut fingers; keep hands away whenever the motors are powered.

## Key terms
- **Quadcopter**: an aircraft supported by four powered propellers.
- **Attitude**: the aircraft’s orientation, described by roll, pitch and yaw.
- **Firmware**: software that runs directly on the robot’s embedded computer.
- **Deck**: Bitcraze’s name for an expansion board adding sensors or other functions.

## Getting started
1. **Access:** documentation and source code are free; availability and cost of an original 2.1 kit are unknown.
2. **Watch** Crazyflie 101, then label the motors, battery, radio and sensor board on the archived product picture.
3. **Trace** a setpoint through the firmware repository to the stabiliser and controller; make a short function-call diagram.
4. **If using existing hardware,** identify its version and follow the matching official assembly and client instructions before attempting a first hover.

## Used in
- **Map connection:** Multirotor flight dynamics & control introduces the forces behind its motor commands.
- **Project connection:** Fly a Crazyflie with the stock cascaded PID uses this platform family; confirm the actual hardware version before following project instructions.

lessons.name: Crazyflie 2.1+
lessons.summary: Crazyflie 2.1+ is Bitcraze’s 29-gram open-source flying development platform for experimenting with sensors, onboard software and flight controllers.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence
Crazyflie 2.1+ is Bitcraze’s 29-gram open-source flying development platform for experimenting with sensors, onboard software and flight controllers.

![Crazyflie 2.1+ with its exposed circuit board, battery and revised propellers](/img/lessons/robots_drone-crazyflie-21-plus.webp)
*Crazyflie 2.1+ with its exposed circuit board, battery and revised propellers. Source: [Bitcraze](https://www.bitcraze.io/products/crazyflie-2-1-plus/), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us
- **A practical control platform:** its public controller implementations let us connect a feedback-control diagram to code running on a real aircraft.
- **An actual revision:** the 2024 launch changed the propellers and battery; it should not silently inherit every number from Bitcraze Crazyflie 2.1.

## What it is made of / how it works
- **Flight hardware:** four motors surround the electronics and battery; an expansion connector accepts optional sensor decks.
- **Software layers:** estimators turn sensor readings into state estimates, then controllers turn target motion into motor commands.
- **Software analogy:** controller selection resembles swapping an implementation behind an interface; the same command still needs compatible assumptions and inputs.
- **Worked example:** 15 g of payload is about half of the 29 g vehicle mass; adding sensors is a major change at this scale.
- **Published figures:** the product page lists the following nominal values; an added deck does not come with a promise of unchanged endurance.

| Specification | Published value |
| --- | --- |
| Mass | 29 g |
| Advertised flight time | 7 min |
| Maximum recommended payload | 15 g |
| Battery charging time | 40 min |
| Radio | 2.4 GHz; BLE also supported |
| Main processor | STM32F405, 168 MHz |

> **Key idea:** A new controller is only meaningful when its required state estimates and command conventions match the rest of the flight stack.

## Key terms
- **Setpoint**: the target value the controller should follow.
- **PID**: proportional, integral and derivative feedback terms used to correct tracking error.
- **Estimator**: software combining measurements into an estimate of position, speed or orientation.
- **Cascaded control**: nested loops where one controller supplies the target for another.

## Getting started
1. **Access:** source and documentation are free; current hardware and complete positioning-kit prices are unknown here.
2. **Follow** the official getting-started videos, including assembly and the successful self-test example; identify any optional deck in your own setup.
3. **Read** the controller documentation and compare PID, Mellinger and INDI at the level of required inputs and intended use.
4. **Write** a simulated error logger with target, estimate and timestamp columns before trying to change any flying controller.

## Used in
- **Foundations:** Feedback control & PID and Multirotor flight control explain the nested loops.
- **Projects:** Fly a Crazyflie with the stock cascaded PID precedes Swap Crazyflie controllers: PID vs Mellinger vs INDI.
- **Later work:** Learning-based & data-driven control connects to RL low-level quadrotor controller sim-to-real.

lessons.name: Delair UX11
lessons.summary: Delair UX11 is a hand-launched fixed-wing drone that gathers aerial photographs for surveying and mapping.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence
Delair UX11 is a hand-launched fixed-wing drone that gathers aerial photographs for surveying and mapping.

![The Delair UX11 flying wing with a rear propeller and integrated camera opening](/img/lessons/robots_drone-delair-ux11.webp)
*The Delair UX11 flying wing with a rear propeller and integrated camera opening. Source: [Delair](https://delair.aero/delair-commercial-drones/professional-mapping-drone-delair-ux11/), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us
- **Flight serves the dataset:** overlapping, well-positioned pictures are useful outputs; merely completing a flight does not produce a trustworthy map.
- **A useful comparison:** unlike a hovering quadcopter, this aircraft cruises on wings and lands on its belly.

## What it is made of / how it works
- **Airframe and camera:** the lightweight wing carries a global-shutter RGB camera; RGB means ordinary red, green and blue colour imaging.
- **Mission software:** Delair’s current sheet names Drako for planning and monitoring, with a checklist and image-quality feedback.
- **Positioning:** satellite measurements can be refined with optional PPK processing, rather than treating every photograph’s initial coordinates as exact.
- **Software analogy:** mapping resembles a build pipeline: capture images, attach position information, then process and validate the resulting map.
- **Worked example:** the published 1.3 cm ground sampling distance means one image pixel represents about 1.3 cm on the ground at 122 m altitude.
- **Configuration:** these figures come from the July 2025 RGB UX11 sheet; infrared variants and older tutorials describe different configurations.

| Specification | Published value |
| --- | --- |
| Mass including payload | 1.6 kg |
| Wingspan | 1.2 m |
| Advertised endurance | Up to 80 min |
| Cruise speed | 54 km/h |
| Camera resolution | 21.4 megapixels |
| Ground sampling distance | 1.3 cm at 122 m altitude |

> **Key idea:** Image resolution describes sampling detail; it does not, by itself, establish the positional accuracy of a finished survey.

## Key terms
- **Fixed-wing**: an aircraft whose wings provide lift while it moves forward.
- **Global shutter**: a camera shutter exposing the whole image at once.
- **GSD**: ground sampling distance, the ground size represented by one image pixel.
- **PPK**: post-processed kinematic positioning, refining satellite positions after data collection.

## Getting started
1. **Access:** the videos and specification sheet are free; a complete UX11 system price is unknown.
2. **Watch** the assembly tutorial and identify the detachable wings, body and camera without treating an old interface as the current software.
3. **Calculate** the footprint of 100 adjacent pixels at the stated GSD: 100 × 1.3 cm = 1.3 m.
4. **Outline** a mock survey checklist with image overlap, location records and image-quality review; no aircraft purchase is needed for this exercise.

## Used in
- **Builder:** Delair presents UX11 for surveying, construction, mining and environmental mapping.
- **Compare:** WingtraRAY targets a similar mapping workflow but uses vertical take-off and landing rather than hand launch and belly landing.

lessons.name: Donecle automated aircraft inspection system
lessons.summary: Donecle automated aircraft inspection system combines autonomous drone photography with image-analysis software and inspection reports for aircraft maintenance.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence
Donecle automated aircraft inspection system combines autonomous drone photography with image-analysis software and inspection reports for aircraft maintenance.

![A Donecle inspection drone photographing an aircraft surface at close range](/img/lessons/robots_drone-donecle.webp)
*A Donecle inspection drone photographing an aircraft surface at close range. Source: [Donecle](https://www.donecle.com/iris-gvi/), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us
- **A focused robotics product:** the useful result is a located, reviewable defect record rather than a drone that simply flies around an aircraft.
- **Relevant to software students:** navigation, image capture, computer vision and report generation have to agree about which aircraft surface each image represents.

## What it is made of / how it works
- **Image acquisition:** a tablet launches the inspection; Donecle describes laser-based positioning without GPS or external positioning sensors.
- **Camera control:** a motorised camera mount follows the aircraft’s curvature while images are collected around its external surface.
- **Analysis and review:** algorithms suggest defects and pre-fill reports; the inspector validates the findings.
- **Software analogy:** picture a test runner that produces candidate failures with exact file locations; a reviewer still decides what each failure means.
- **Worked example:** an image marked as a possible defect must keep its aircraft location and inspection date, so a later inspection can revisit that finding.
- **Vendor claims:** figures below concern the overall system; the dent figure specifically requires the Iris 3D sensor configuration.

| Specification | Published value |
| --- | --- |
| Narrowbody inspection | Less than 1 hour |
| Positioning | Centimetric, laser-based |
| Advertised defect detection | Down to 1 mm² |
| Iris 3D dent-depth accuracy | Down to 0.1 mm |

> **Key idea:** An inspection system must preserve evidence and location from camera capture through human review and maintenance reporting.

## Key terms
- **Narrowbody**: a single-aisle passenger aircraft category.
- **Gimbal**: a movable mount that controls the camera’s viewing direction.
- **General visual inspection**: a visual check of condition, abbreviated GVI.
- **Traceability**: keeping enough linked evidence to reconstruct where a finding came from.

## Getting started
1. **Access:** public demonstrations and product descriptions are free; the commercial system price and student access are unknown.
2. **Watch** the scan sequence and separate flight automation from the subsequent image-analysis and reporting stages.
3. **Design** a JSON finding with an image reference, surface location, proposed defect type and reviewer decision; use dummy records.
4. **Build** a small review page that preserves the original suggestion when a reviewer changes its status, then compare it with Donecle’s workflow.

## Used in
- **Builder:** Donecle offers aircraft inspections covering defects, paint wear, regulatory markings and lightning-strike evidence.
- **Compare:** Elios 3 also links inspection observations to spatial context, but is designed for confined-space access.

lessons.name: Elios 3
lessons.summary: Elios 3 is Flyability’s caged inspection drone for collecting images, spatial maps and specialised measurements inside confined spaces.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence
Elios 3 is Flyability’s caged inspection drone for collecting images, spatial maps and specialised measurements inside confined spaces.

![Elios 3 inside its protective cage, with forward-facing cameras and lighting](/img/lessons/robots_drone-elios-3.webp)
*Elios 3 inside its protective cage, with forward-facing cameras and lighting. Source: [Flyability](https://www.flyability.com/elios-3), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us
- **A different environment:** indoor tanks, tunnels and industrial interiors require localisation without depending on satellite reception.
- **Mechanical design helps software:** the cage and collision-recovery controller make contact with the surroundings a design consideration rather than an entirely unexpected event.

## What it is made of / how it works
- **Protective cage:** a surrounding frame protects the aircraft during contact; Flyability also describes a controller and reversing propellers for collision recovery.
- **Localisation:** LiDAR, visual-inertial cameras and SLAM help estimate motion and construct a map in places without GPS.
- **Inspection payloads:** visual and thermal imaging can be complemented by surveying, ultrasonic thickness or radiation-measurement equipment.
- **Software analogy:** Inspector attaches findings to locations in a digital model, like linking a bug report to the exact part of a codebase.
- **Worked example:** a visual photograph can flag a suspicious pipe area; an ultrasonic payload addresses a different question, the remaining wall thickness.
- **Read the configuration:** the original launch video specifies the standard visual setup; newer payloads and batteries change the system.

| Specification | Published value |
| --- | --- |
| Standard setup in launch video | Up to 12.5 min flight |
| Built-in visible camera | 4K |
| Lighting in launch video | Up to 16,000 lumens |
| Mapping output | Real-time 3D point cloud |
| Navigation | LiDAR and visual-inertial SLAM; GPS not required |

> **Key idea:** Reaching an inaccessible space, knowing where the robot is, and measuring an asset’s condition are three distinct jobs.

## Key terms
- **LiDAR**: a sensor using laser light to measure distances.
- **SLAM**: simultaneous localisation and mapping, estimating position while building a map.
- **Point cloud**: many measured 3D points representing surrounding surfaces.
- **UT**: ultrasonic testing, using sound waves to measure material thickness.

## Getting started
1. **Access:** public videos and payload descriptions are free; a complete aircraft package price is unknown.
2. **Watch** the launch demonstration and identify cage, lighting, camera feed and map as separate parts of the system.
3. **Make** a dummy inspection record joining a photo filename, a 3D coordinate and an inspector’s comment.
4. **Compare** surveying and UT payload pages, then choose which output would answer a geometry question versus a thickness question.

## Used in
- **Builder:** Flyability links Elios 3 data to Inspector for spatially organised inspection records.
- **Compare:** Donecle automated aircraft inspection system focuses on aircraft surfaces; Voliro T adds controlled aerial contact for measurement.

lessons.name: EXRAY
lessons.summary: EXRAY is Hydromea’s underwater inspection robot for viewing and measuring submerged structures, including tight industrial spaces.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence
EXRAY is Hydromea’s underwater inspection robot for viewing and measuring submerged structures, including tight industrial spaces.

![Hydromea’s yellow-and-black EXRAY underwater inspection robot](/img/lessons/robots_drone-exray.webp)
*Hydromea’s yellow-and-black EXRAY underwater inspection robot. Source: [Hydromea](https://www.hydromea.com/exray-underwater-robot), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us
- **An underwater drone:** its job is inspection below the surface, where the communication link and access route are central design constraints.
- **Useful data has context:** Hydromea’s NAVIA software associates findings with inspection positions instead of leaving the operator with an unstructured video recording.

## What it is made of / how it works
- **Vehicle and payloads:** thrusters move the robot; a tilting camera records video and still images, with optional sonar and thickness-measurement payloads.
- **Six degrees of freedom:** the vehicle can translate and rotate in three dimensions, supporting inspection from different orientations.
- **Optional FLYOUT:** a small untethered robot uses LUMA optical communication with the tethered ROV, which acts as a relay.
- **Software analogy:** FLYOUT resembles a remote worker reached through a gateway; removing its cable does not remove the communication dependency.
- **Worked example:** the advertised FLYOUT distance is up to 30 m from its relay; that is different from the main robot’s 100 m supplied tether.
- **Manufacturer figures:** the product FAQ labels some specifications preliminary, so configuration details need checking for a real deployment.

| Specification | Published value |
| --- | --- |
| ROV mass | 9 kg |
| Depth rating | 200 m |
| Typical endurance | 6 hours |
| Supplied tether | 100 m |
| Optional FLYOUT link | Up to 30 m from tethered relay |
| Camera output | Full HD video; 4K still images |

> **Key idea:** An untethered inspection vehicle still needs an explicit plan for communication, navigation and the return path.

## Key terms
- **ROV**: remotely operated vehicle, controlled by an operator rather than necessarily completing its mission alone.
- **Thruster**: a propeller unit producing force to move or turn an underwater robot.
- **Optical communication**: transmitting information with light.
- **NDT**: nondestructive testing, measuring condition without cutting the inspected part apart.

## Getting started
1. **Access:** demonstrations and application pages are free; complete system and optional-payload prices are unknown.
2. **Watch** the introduction, then the ballast-tank case; identify which part of the work is performed by the operator.
3. **Draw** the data route from robot to relay to operator and label which link carries a tether.
4. **Build** a dummy inspection log linking frame, component name and finding; treat loss of the communication link as a separate state.

## Used in
- **Builder:** Hydromea shows EXRAY inspecting ballast tanks and hydropower structures.
- **Compare:** Tethys One emphasises underwater positioning in currents; Seasam combines underwater inspection with its own software and reporting tools.

lessons.name: Fotokite Sigma
lessons.summary: Fotokite Sigma is a powered-tether camera drone that provides first responders with a persistent elevated colour and thermal view.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence
Fotokite Sigma is a powered-tether camera drone that provides first responders with a persistent elevated colour and thermal view.

![Fotokite Sigma aircraft stowed on its portable transport-case ground station](/img/lessons/robots_drone-fotokite-sigma.webp)
*Fotokite Sigma aircraft stowed on its portable transport-case ground station. Source: [Fotokite](https://fotokite.com/transport-case/), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us
- **An intentionally constrained robot:** the tether supplies power and communication, trading free travel for a persistent view above an incident.
- **A clear product goal:** responders need situational awareness, meaning an understandable view of what is happening around them, rather than arbitrary aerial manoeuvres.

## What it is made of / how it works
- **Aircraft and ground station:** the rotorcraft launches from a case or vehicle-mounted system and remains connected by a reinforced cable.
- **Two image streams:** the colour camera shows visible detail while the thermal camera gives complementary heat-related information.
- **Automation:** Fotokite describes automatic launch, flight and landing with no GPS dependency; its Live application displays imagery and system status.
- **Software analogy:** a wired peripheral can simplify power and data management, but its cable also defines where it can operate.
- **Worked example:** a 45 m maximum height is measured from the ground station; it does not imply a freely roaming 45 m survey radius.
- **Configuration:** the following figures are for the published Transport Case system and depend on continuing ground power.

| Specification | Published value |
| --- | --- |
| Aircraft take-off mass | 1.3 kg |
| Continuous operation claim | 24 hours with vehicle or shore power |
| Maximum height | 45 m from ground station |
| Thermal stream | 320 × 240 at 27 frames/s |
| Colour stream | 1920 × 1080 at 30 frames/s |
| Case-system mass | 19.5 kg |
| Weather rating | IP55 |

> **Key idea:** Constraining a robot’s movement can simplify the system enough to deliver a more useful service for a specific task.

## Key terms
- **Tether**: the cable connecting aircraft and ground equipment.
- **Ground station**: the equipment providing the aircraft’s ground-side power, communication and control functions.
- **Thermal image**: an image formed from detected infrared radiation.
- **Frame rate**: the number of video images produced each second.

## Getting started
1. **Access:** public demonstrations and specifications are free; the commercial system price and student access are unknown.
2. **Watch** the responder overview, then identify aircraft, tether, ground station and display in the product images.
3. **List** the consequences of ground power loss versus video-network loss; the specification describes separate backup power and recovery features.
4. **Mock up** an incident dashboard with colour video, thermal video and connection status as separate panels, using placeholders rather than a real aircraft.

## Used in
- **Builder:** Fotokite presents Sigma for firefighting, law enforcement and incident response.
- **Compare:** ANAFI UKR is a free-flying observation aircraft; Skeyetech combines repeated sorties with a charging dock.

lessons.name: iBubble
lessons.summary: iBubble is Notilo Plus’s underwater camera robot, designed to follow a diver and position an action camera during a dive.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence
iBubble is Notilo Plus’s underwater camera robot, designed to follow a diver and position an action camera during a dive.

![The yellow iBubble underwater drone in Notilo Plus’s published product image](/img/lessons/robots_drone-ibubble.webp)
*The yellow iBubble underwater drone in Notilo Plus’s published product image. Source: [Notilo Plus](https://www.notiloplus.com/), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us
- **A concrete interaction task:** a diver asks for a filming viewpoint while the robot handles following and stabilisation underwater.
- **Evidence beyond promotion:** Fisheries and Oceans Canada published preliminary trials of iBubble for seabed imaging, including practical limitations of that different task.

## What it is made of / how it works
- **Following:** the research note describes an acoustic transmitter carried by the diver and onboard visual recognition supporting relative tracking.
- **Movement:** seven propellers stabilise and reposition the vehicle; the diver can request different filming positions.
- **Recording:** the built-in camera supports tracking and live viewing; the Canadian trials used a separate Paralenz action camera to record images.
- **Software analogy:** this is a moving camera service whose target is another moving object; the target’s position is an input that must be measured repeatedly.
- **Worked example:** a request to film from the diver’s side needs a relative position, not merely a fixed depth command.
- **Historical specifications:** the table reports the 2021 research note’s description of its tested equipment, not a claim about current stock or revised models.

| Specification | Published value |
| --- | --- |
| Propellers | 7 |
| Reported maximum depth | 60 m |
| Reported maximum speed | 1.5 m/s |
| Lights | Two 1,000-lumen lamps |
| Control modes | Autonomous following; ROV mode with Explorer pack |

> **Key idea:** Following a moving subject and recording scientifically consistent imagery are different requirements, even when they use the same robot.

## Key terms
- **Acoustic link**: communication using sound through water.
- **Relative tracking**: estimating where a target is compared with the robot itself.
- **ROV mode**: direct remote operation rather than autonomous following.
- **Transect**: a planned survey path used to collect observations along a defined line.

## Getting started
1. **Access:** the public research note and demonstration are free; current purchase availability and complete-system price are unknown.
2. **Watch** the diver-following demonstration, then distinguish the filming camera from sensors helping the robot follow.
3. **Read** the Canadian trials’ methods and results; note where a diver-following design helps or complicates seabed survey work.
4. **Write** a mock tracker accepting diver-relative position and desired viewing side; output a desired relative viewpoint, without pretending it is a working underwater controller.

## Used in
- **Builder:** Notilo Plus presents iBubble alongside its professional Seasam platform.
- **Compare:** Seasam focuses on industrial inspection and reporting; the Canadian iBubble study explores adapting a diver-filming product to research.
